prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms brought time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B027 as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye. The discovery is the magic-wavelength condition: choosing the lattice wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock states cancel lets many atoms be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime with no Doppler or recoil broadening. That is a new regime of control, not a refinement of a comb or an ion clock, and neither the 2005 nor the 2012 prize covers neutral atoms confined in a lattice. The claim has been reproduced by independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others), the 1e-18 level is established by clock-to-clock comparisons, and the same instruments now give millimetre-scale gravitational redshift tests and many-body clock physics (spin exchange, correlated lattice gases). The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and leaves one place free. I cannot see the committee having a stronger candidate this year in terms of discovery, reproducibility and attribution taken together. I have moved no further than round 1 on the configuration, but the chair's questions have sharpened how I would word the citation and why I do not think waiting for the SI redefinition is necessary.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 (Hall, Hansch) and 2012 (Wineland, Haroche) is real, and Danielsson and Kroll are right that a citation phrased only as better clocks would read as a third award in one neighbourhood. The deliverable results about nature are so far bounds and redshift tests, not a surprise, so Lindroth's point that the discovery content is a capability has weight. Ye's contribution is arguably a decisive development of Katori's idea, and Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Oates are outside the credit. Finally the second has not been redefined, so one can argue that the committee is acting a little early. I judge these to be reasons for careful wording and not for a different choice.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B057 first, argues that Kane-Mele and Molenkamp gave a symmetry-protected classification of real band insulators that is distinct from the 2016 prize, and acknowledges that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D omissions are the real weakness and that B027 has broader first-tier support.
responses.response: I cannot judge the band-topology physics myself, and your answer on 2016, topological invariants in models and phase transitions versus a classification of real materials with a decisive measurement, is a good one. My difficulty is the credit rather than the merit. You and Mehlig both say that an honest citation would have to be worded around Z2 and the first observation without implying that the HgTe prediction is unrecognised, and Zhang's death means that gap cannot be repaired. With B027 the committee can name the idea and the demonstration in two names and defend it fully. What would move me toward B057 is a convincing statement from you or Mehlig that the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio would stand even if Bernevig and Hughes were left out, and I would hold it as my second choice for now.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube to B027, wants the wording to rest on what the precision has shown (redshift tests, many-body physics), and says that Ye's credit overlaps with the comb and cavity-stabilisation work touched by the 2005 prize.
responses.response: I agree about the wording and I would now write it into the citation: the discovery is magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, with the 1e-18 level as the demonstration, and the redshift and many-body work as consequences. On Ye, I think the overlap you describe is a real concern for his career in general but not for this credit, because his stabilised-laser and comb expertise was a tool and the lattice-clock accuracy and spin-exchange physics were achieved in the lattice. I would resist the stronger form of your instrument objection: a clock that resolves a gravitational potential difference over a millimetre is already a measurement of nature, and the quantum-many-body behaviour of the lattice gas is physics in its own right, not just metrology.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye is the originator or the developer of Katori's concept, whether Takamoto, Ludlow or others have claims that disturb the two-name credit, and notes that the redefinition of the second has not happened.
responses.response: My reading is that Katori is the originator of the magic-wavelength lattice idea, which he proposed in 2001 and then demonstrated for strontium, and that Ye's decisive contribution was to take the scheme to a new accuracy regime and to develop the many-body and spin-exchange physics, which is why the citation should say invention and development, as Lindroth suggests. Takamoto's 2005 demonstration was in Katori's group, so it belongs to the same line, and Ludlow and Oates are in the Ye and NIST ecosystem and are better described as the continued development than as a rival origin. I do not think a third name is justified, and with the three-person limit I would rather keep the pair than weaken it. On timing, the science is established at 1e-18 without the redefinition, and waiting a cycle risks nothing but would gain nothing either.

responses.point: Kroll says the clock will not be harmed by waiting a cycle and asks whether to wait for the redefinition of the second, and he places the weight on discoveries that change what matter can be.
responses.response: I understand the argument that a technique prize can wait, but I think it misjudges what is at stake: the lattice clock has already changed what we know about matter in the form of many-body physics with controlled atoms, and the 1e-18 comparisons are a new regime of measurement. The redefinition of the second is a metrological decision and does not change the physics, so I would not tie a Nobel decision to it. I also recognise your point that applications such as geodesy and dark matter are promises, so the citation should not mention them.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see the magic-wavelength scheme as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I think it is, but the committee as a whole may not.
Whether Ye's role is judged as invention or decisive development, and if the committee wants a third name I do not see a clearly stronger candidate.

Whether B057 could be made defensible with a different set of names given Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, which I cannot judge, and whether a two-part prize of B027 and B057 would exceed the three-person limit (it would, with five names).
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work on superconducting circuit QED at Chalmers, so I have a clear connection to B036 and some to B060, and I would recuse on B036. I have no connection to B027, B057 or B006 that I know of. Chalmers has hosted 2025 laureates as guest researchers, which does not bear on these entries. My disclosure is unchanged since round 1.
